title: Two Fights Before Labor Day
author: The Principal's Chair
summary: In this reflective piece from The Principal's Chair, an anonymous school leader recounts treating two student fights, eleven days apart and in different parts of the building, as unconnected incidents, only to discover on a closer read of the paperwork that both occurred in the exact same twelve-minute supervision gap between first bell and homeroom. The essay traces how a July bus-schedule change quietly widened that gap by six minutes without anyone updating staff duty assignments, and how two vacant duty posts from a spring retirement had never been reflected on the schedule itself. The author's broader argument is that behavior clusters around time and place before it clusters around cause, and that treating discipline incidents as one-off, individual problems can mask underlying structural failures in supervision and scheduling. The piece ends with the leader's fix, reassigning teachers to cover the gap and building a standing habit of re-reading incident reports against a rolling window of prior referrals, offered as a transferable practice for any school leader auditing incident patterns.
points: A principal's after-the-fact review of two 'unrelated' fights revealed both occurred in the same unsupervised twelve-minute gap between first bell and homeroom — a structural scheduling failure, not a discipline problem.

The gap had silently widened by six minutes after a July bus-schedule change, and staff duty assignments were never updated to match, showing how operational drift outside the classroom creates disciplinary risk.

Argues that behavior clusters around time and place before it clusters around cause, so incident reports should be checked against a rolling thirty-day window of time and location data rather than treated as isolated events.
The fix was structural — reassigning two teachers with open first-period preps to cover the gap — rather than punitive, and it eliminated repeat incidents in that window.

Institutionalizes a low-cost habit, a second morning read of every incident report cross-checked against recent referrals, that already caught a second emerging pattern before it became a bigger story.
quotes: Two fights in eleven school days, before Labor Day even arrived. I told the superintendent both were unrelated. I was wrong about that before the ink dried on my own report.

Both fights happened during the same twelve-minute window, the unsupervised stretch between the first bell and when homeroom attendance officially started, a gap that had grown by six minutes when the district shifted the bus schedule in July and nobody adjusted staff duty assignments to match.

I pulled the duty schedule and mapped every adult's actual location during that window, not their assigned location, the actual one. Two duty posts had quietly gone unfilled since a retirement in the spring that nobody had backfilled on the schedule itself, only in the budget line.
I reassigned two teachers with open first-period preps to cover that window starting the next Monday. No fight has happened in that twelve-minute stretch since.

But behavior clusters around time and place before it clusters around cause. A school leader who checks the clock and the map before accepting the easy explanation catches structural gaps that a second, third, or fourth incident will otherwise reveal the hard way.

I built a standing habit out of it too. Every incident report now gets a second read the following morning, specifically checking time and location against the last thirty days of referrals, before I sign off and call it closed.
